How I Did It: Pac-Chase

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Pac-Man landed in my place in the fall of 1980 and by Christmas I had two of them and a waiting line anyway. There was a girl named Denise, maybe eleven, who kept a spiral notebook of ghost patterns — she'd stand there not even playing, just watching other people lose and writing down why. By '82 she could run the first board with her eyes half closed. I think about that notebook every time somebody tells me the ghosts are "just random." They never were.

What the remodel changed

The '25 version of this one moved everybody a whole square at a time, like checkers. Worked, but it felt like checkers too. This time the robots made everything glide — your guy is always somewhere between two tiles, moving at a real speed in pixels per second, and the game only asks "which way now?" when he crosses a tile's center. The big one is the buffered turn: you can press UP a half-second before the corner and the game holds onto it and fires it the instant the turn is legal. That's the thing that made the real cabinet feel like it was reading your mind. And each ghost got its own brain back — the red one hunts you, the pink one aims ahead of you, the blue one flanks, and the orange one loses his nerve up close. Same as Denise's notebook said.

The spell that did it

Rebuild Pac-Chase on the shared engine and make it faithful. I want the four ghost personalities from the real game — chaser, ambusher, flanker, and the shy one — with the scatter/chase mode swaps where they all reverse direction. Movement has to be smooth between tiles, and buffer my turns so pressing early still takes the corner. Power pellets turn them blue, they flash before it wears off, eaten ghosts become eyes that walk home. Fruit under the ghost house, extra life at 10,000. Make eating dots sound like something.

Under the hood

  • The maze is one array of 31 text strings, 28 characters wide — walls, dots, pellets, the ghost-house door — and I had the robots prove it's left-right symmetric and fully connected before a single ghost walked it.
  • Everybody moves at tiles-per-second speeds multiplied by the engine's fixed time step, so a slow laptop and a fast one play the exact same game.
  • At every tile center a ghost looks at its legal exits, throws out the one behind it, and picks whichever is closest in a straight line to its personal target square. Four different targets, four different personalities — that's the whole trick.
  • Eating a power pellet flips the ghosts around and starts a timer that gets shorter every level, and the 200-400-800-1600 chain for eating them in one pellet is in there, floating numbers and all.
